title: What an Eight-Week Schedule Pilot Shows
text:
Lumen Design tested a four-day work schedule with one project team for eight weeks. Employees worked the same total weekly hours across four longer days and kept Friday free unless a client emergency required coverage. Team manager Celia Ortiz argues that the company has enough evidence to continue testing the schedule, but not enough to declare it successful company-wide.

During the pilot, the team completed 27 client tasks compared with 25 during the previous eight-week period. Average response time to routine client messages changed from 3.8 hours to 3.6 hours. Employees used six unscheduled absence days during the pilot, compared with eleven in the previous period. In an anonymous survey, 14 of the 16 team members said they would prefer to keep the schedule.

The pilot does not establish that the schedule caused each difference. The team had one fewer large project than in the earlier period, and a new project-management tool was introduced during week three. The sample was also small and came from a group whose work could often be scheduled in advance. Customer-support teams that handle live requests may face different constraints.

Ortiz therefore supports a second pilot with two additional teams and clearer measures of client coverage. She opposes a memo circulated by one supervisor claiming, “The trial proves that a four-day week increases productivity and will reduce absences across every department.” Ortiz says the evidence is promising, but the memo turns a limited pilot into a much broader conclusion than the data can support.
